_about: Hand-written descriptions for vessels the Wikipedia import left without one. Keyed by exact structure name; see app/extra_content.py.

Accessory branch of middle meningeal art.description:
A small branch of the maxillary artery (or of the middle meningeal artery itself) that ascends through the foramen ovale into the middle cranial fossa.
Outside the skull it supplies the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles, tensor veli palatini and the auditory tube; inside, it supplies the trigeminal ganglion and adjacent dura.

Accessory hemi-azygos vein.description:
Longitudinal vein on the left side of the thoracic vertebral bodies that drains the 4th to 8th left posterior intercostal veins (and often the left bronchial veins).
It descends to about T7-T8, where it crosses behind the aorta, oesophagus and thoracic duct to join the azygos vein; it frequently communicates with the hemi-azygos vein below and the left superior intercostal vein above.

Anterior circumflex humeral artery.description:
Smaller of the two circumflex humeral arteries, arising from the third part of the axillary artery. It passes laterally in front of the surgical neck of the humerus, deep to coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps, and anastomoses with the posterior circumflex humeral artery.
Its ascending (arcuate) branch runs up the intertubercular groove and is the main supply of the humeral head, so it is at risk in displaced proximal humeral fractures.

Anterior deep temporal artery.description: Branch of the second (pterygoid) part of the maxillary artery that ascends between the temporalis muscle and the temporal fossa to supply the anterior part of temporalis. Small branches pass through the zygomatic bone to anastomose with the lacrimal artery.

Posterior deep temporal artery.description: Branch of the second (pterygoid) part of the maxillary artery that ascends deep to the temporalis muscle, supplying its posterior part and anastomosing with the middle temporal branch of the superficial temporal artery.

Anterior division of internal iliac arte.description:
The larger of the two trunks into which the internal iliac artery divides at the upper border of the greater sciatic foramen. It runs down along the pelvic side wall and gives mainly visceral branches: the umbilical artery (with the superior vesical arteries), obturator, inferior vesical (male) or vaginal and uterine (female), middle rectal, internal pudendal and inferior gluteal arteries.
It supplies the bladder, internal genital organs, rectum, perineum and the medial thigh and buttock; it is the vessel embolised or ligated to control severe pelvic or post-partum haemorrhage.

Anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal ar.description:
Branch of the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from the superior mesenteric artery) that runs to the right across the front of the head of the pancreas, in the groove against the duodenum.
It anastomoses with the anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from the gastroduodenal artery), forming the anterior pancreaticoduodenal arcade - an important collateral path between the coeliac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery.

Anterior interventricular artery.description:
The left anterior descending (LAD) artery: continuation of the left coronary artery that runs in the anterior interventricular groove toward the apex, often wrapping around it onto the inferior surface.
Through its diagonal branches and septal perforators it supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle, the apex and the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, including the bundle branches. Proximal occlusion causes an extensive anterior infarction (the so-called widow-maker) with ST elevation in V1-V4.

Septal branches of anterior interventric.description:
Perforating branches that leave the underside of the left anterior descending artery at right angles and plunge into the interventricular septum. They supply the anterior two-thirds of the septum, including the bundle of His and the bundle branches.
The first septal perforator is the vessel injected with alcohol in septal ablation for hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

Right inferolateral branch of right coro.description: Branch of the distal right coronary artery given off at or beyond the crux of the heart (also called the right posterolateral branch). In right-dominant hearts it supplies the inferior (diaphragmatic) and inferolateral wall of the left ventricle, so its occlusion contributes to inferior and inferolateral infarcts.

Inferior vein of left ventricle.description: Also called the posterior vein of the left ventricle. It ascends on the diaphragmatic surface of the left ventricle and drains into the coronary sinus (sometimes into the great cardiac vein), returning blood from the inferior and inferolateral left ventricular wall. It is one of the veins used to place a left ventricular pacing lead in cardiac resynchronisation therapy.

Inferior vein of left ventricle (//Poste.description: Also called the posterior vein of the left ventricle. It ascends on the diaphragmatic surface of the left ventricle and drains into the coronary sinus (sometimes into the great cardiac vein), returning blood from the inferior and inferolateral left ventricular wall. It is one of the veins used to place a left ventricular pacing lead in cardiac resynchronisation therapy.

Anterior papillary muscle of right ventr.description:
The largest papillary muscle of the right ventricle, rising from the anterior wall. Its chordae tendineae pass to the anterior and posterior (inferior) leaflets of the tricuspid valve.
The septomarginal trabecula (moderator band) runs from the septum to its base, carrying the right bundle branch, so the muscle contracts early and tenses the chordae before ventricular pressure rises.

Inferior papillary muscle of right ventr.description: The posterior (inferior) papillary muscle of the right ventricle, arising from the inferior wall. Often made of two or three parts, its chordae tendineae pass to the posterior (inferior) and septal leaflets of the tricuspid valve and prevent their eversion during systole.

Septal papillary muscle of right ventric.description: Small, variable papillary muscle (sometimes just chordae) arising from the interventricular septum of the right ventricle. The most constant part is the medial papillary muscle of the conus (of Lancisi), whose chordae go to the anterior and septal leaflets of the tricuspid valve; it marks the position of the right bundle branch.

Inferior papillary muscle of left ventri.description:
The posteromedial papillary muscle of the left ventricle, arising from the inferior wall. Its chordae tendineae go to both mitral leaflets (medial halves).
Because it usually has a single blood supply from the posterior interventricular artery, it is the papillary muscle most prone to ischaemic dysfunction or rupture after an inferior myocardial infarction, causing acute mitral regurgitation.

Anterior semilunar leaflet of pulmonary.description: One of the three semilunar cusps of the pulmonary valve, lying anteriorly. Like the others it has a thickened nodule at the middle of its free edge and thin crescentic lunules on either side; the cusps close together in early diastole, producing the pulmonary component (P2) of the second heart sound.

Left semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valv.description: One of the three semilunar cusps of the pulmonary valve, on the left and posteriorly, facing the left coronary cusp of the aortic valve. Each cusp bulges into a pulmonary sinus; closure of the cusps in early diastole produces the pulmonary component (P2) of the second heart sound.

Right semilunar leaflet of pulmonary val.description: One of the three semilunar cusps of the pulmonary valve, on the right and posteriorly, facing the right coronary cusp of the aortic valve. Its free edge carries a central nodule and lateral lunules that seal against the other two cusps when the valve closes in early diastole.

Right coronary leaflet.description: The right (anterior) cusp of the aortic valve. The right aortic sinus behind it gives rise to the right coronary artery, whose ostium lies just below the sinotubular junction. The cusps fill with blood and coronary flow is greatest during diastole, when the aortic valve is closed.

Non-coronary leaflet.description: The posterior (right posterior) cusp of the aortic valve, so called because its sinus gives rise to no coronary artery. It lies against the interatrial septum; beneath its junction with the right coronary cusp lies the membranous septum and the bundle of His, which is why aortic valve disease, surgery and transcatheter valve implantation can cause heart block.

Posterior leaflet of left atrioventricul.description:
The posterior (mural) leaflet of the mitral valve: long and narrow, attached to about two-thirds of the annulus circumference and usually divided into three scallops (P1-P3). Chordae from both papillary muscles attach to it.
Mitral valve prolapse most often involves P2, and the posterior leaflet is the one usually repaired surgically.

Inferior leaflet of right atrioventricul.description: The posterior (inferior) leaflet of the tricuspid valve, attached along the inferior margin of the annulus near the diaphragmatic surface. Its chordae come from the posterior (inferior) and anterior papillary muscles.

Septal leaflet of right atrioventricular.description: The tricuspid leaflet attached to the interventricular septum, with chordae from the septal and posterior papillary muscles. Its hinge line is set slightly toward the apex compared with the anterior mitral leaflet (the normal offset); an exaggerated apical displacement is the hallmark of Ebstein anomaly. The AV node and bundle of His lie close to its attachment.

Anterior septal branches of anterior eth.description: Branches of the anterior ethmoidal artery (from the ophthalmic artery) that supply the anterosuperior part of the nasal septum. They contribute to Kiesselbach's plexus in Little's area, the commonest source of anterior epistaxis, and represent an internal carotid contribution to the nasal blood supply.

Septal branches of posterior ethmoidal a.description: Small branches of the posterior ethmoidal artery (from the ophthalmic artery) that reach the upper posterior nasal septum through the cribriform plate region, supplying the septal mucosa near the olfactory area.

Posterior lateral nasal branches of sphe.description: Branches of the sphenopalatine artery (terminal part of the maxillary artery) that enter the nose through the sphenopalatine foramen and fan out over the conchae and meatuses of the lateral nasal wall, also supplying the maxillary, ethmoidal and sphenoidal sinuses. They are the usual source of posterior epistaxis; endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation targets them.

Anterior temporal branch.description: Cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery, usually from its inferior division, that runs out of the lateral sulcus onto the anterior part of the temporal lobe. It supplies the anterior superior, middle and inferior temporal gyri and the temporal pole.

Posterior temporal branch.description: Cortical branch of the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery that runs backward over the posterior temporal lobe. It supplies the posterior superior and middle temporal gyri, including Wernicke's area in the dominant hemisphere; occlusion causes a fluent (Wernicke) aphasia and a contralateral upper quadrantanopia.

Temporo-occipital branch.description: Terminal cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery that runs to the posterior temporal lobe and lateral occipital surface, supplying the posterior temporal gyri and lateral occipital cortex and bordering the territory of the posterior cerebral artery.

Branch to angular gyrus.description: Terminal continuation of the middle cerebral artery (angular artery) emerging from the posterior end of the lateral sulcus. It supplies the angular gyrus and adjacent parietal and occipital cortex; infarction in the dominant hemisphere can cause alexia with agraphia and Gerstmann syndrome (finger agnosia, left-right confusion, agraphia, acalculia).

Artery of central sulcus.description: The Rolandic artery: a cortical (M4) branch of the superior division of the middle cerebral artery that ascends in or along the central sulcus. It supplies the adjacent precentral and postcentral gyri - the face and arm areas of the primary motor and sensory cortex - so its occlusion causes contralateral face and arm weakness and sensory loss.

Artery of precentral sulcus.description: The prerolandic artery: a cortical branch of the superior division of the middle cerebral artery that ascends along the precentral sulcus. It supplies the posterior middle and inferior frontal gyri and the premotor cortex; on the dominant side its territory includes the posterior part of Broca's area.

Postcentral arterial branch.description: The artery of the postcentral sulcus (anterior parietal artery): a cortical branch of the superior division of the middle cerebral artery that ascends along the postcentral sulcus to supply the postcentral gyrus and the anterior part of the parietal lobe.

Posterior parietal artery.description: Cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery that emerges from the posterior lateral sulcus and runs up over the supramarginal gyrus and superior parietal lobule, supplying the posterior parietal cortex.

Prefrontal artery.description: Cortical branch of the superior division of the middle cerebral artery (a candelabra branch) that runs forward and upward over the lateral surface of the frontal lobe, supplying the inferior and middle frontal gyri, including the pars triangularis and opercularis (Broca's area) on the dominant side.

Lateral frontobasal artery.description: The lateral orbitofrontal artery, usually the first cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery. It runs forward on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe, supplying the lateral orbital gyri and the pars orbitalis of the inferior frontal gyrus.

Orbitofrontal branches of anterior cereb.description: The medial orbitofrontal artery and its branches, arising from the proximal A2 segment of the anterior cerebral artery. They run forward on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe to supply the gyrus rectus, olfactory bulb and tract and the medial orbital gyri.

Frontal branches of callosomarginal arte.description: Anteromedial, intermediomedial and posteromedial frontal branches of the callosomarginal artery (a branch of the anterior cerebral artery) that run in the cingulate sulcus and climb over the medial surface of the hemisphere. They supply the superior frontal gyrus and the medial frontal cortex up to the paracentral lobule, whose ischaemia gives weakness mainly of the contralateral leg.

Insular branches of middle cerebral arte.description: The M2 (insular) segment of the middle cerebral artery: the superior and inferior divisions and their branches that lie on the surface of the insula after the MCA turns up at the limen insulae. They supply the insular cortex and give rise to the cortical branches that emerge through the lateral sulcus.

The M2 (insular) segment of the middle cerebral artery: the superior and inferior divisions and their branches that lie on the surface of the insula after the MCA turns up at the limen insulae. They supply the insular cortex and give rise to the cortical branches that emerge through the lateral sulcus.

Middle cerebral artery (M3 segment).description: The opercular (M3) segment of the middle cerebral artery: the branches that loop around the inner surfaces of the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula from the insula to the lips of the lateral sulcus, before emerging as cortical (M4) branches on the lateral surface of the hemisphere.

Middle cerebral artery (M3-segment).description: The opercular (M3) segment of the middle cerebral artery: the branches that loop around the inner surfaces of the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula from the insula to the lips of the lateral sulcus, before emerging as cortical (M4) branches on the lateral surface of the hemisphere.

Parietal branches of middle cerebral art.description: Cortical branches of the middle cerebral artery (anterior and posterior parietal arteries and the angular artery) that supply the lateral surface of the parietal lobe. Dominant-side infarction impairs language and calculation; non-dominant parietal infarction produces contralateral neglect.

Temporal branches of middle cerebral art.description: Cortical branches of the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery (anterior, middle and posterior temporal arteries) that supply the lateral surface of the temporal lobe, including the auditory cortex and, on the dominant side, Wernicke's area.

Proximal lateral striate branches.description:
Lenticulostriate arteries arising from the M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery that pierce the anterior perforated substance. They are end arteries supplying the putamen, lateral globus pallidus, the upper internal capsule and the body of the caudate nucleus.
Their occlusion causes lacunar infarcts (pure motor stroke), and in chronic hypertension they are the classic source of intracerebral haemorrhage into the putamen.

Distal lateral striate branches.description: The more lateral lenticulostriate arteries, arising from the distal M1 segment (or early M2) of the middle cerebral artery and piercing the anterior perforated substance. They supply the lateral putamen, external capsule and the upper posterior limb of the internal capsule; as end arteries they are prone to lacunar infarction and hypertensive haemorrhage.

Medial pontine branches of basilar arter.description: Paramedian perforating branches that leave the back of the basilar artery and enter the pons near the midline. They supply the medial basis pontis (corticospinal fibres and pontine nuclei) and the medial tegmentum (medial lemniscus, abducens fibres); occlusion produces a medial pontine syndrome with contralateral hemiparesis.

Lateral pontine branches of basilar arte.description: Short circumferential branches of the basilar artery that wind around the side of the pons, supplying its anterolateral part including the middle cerebellar peduncle region and the emerging trigeminal fibres.

Artery of pterygoid canal.description: The Vidian artery: a small branch of the third (pterygopalatine) part of the maxillary artery that runs backward through the pterygoid canal with the nerve of the pterygoid canal. It supplies the upper pharynx, auditory tube and tympanic cavity and may anastomose with the petrous internal carotid artery.

Ascending branch of left colic artery.description: Upper branch of the left colic artery (from the inferior mesenteric artery). It ascends in front of the left kidney toward the splenic flexure, supplying the distal transverse and descending colon and anastomosing with the middle colic artery through the marginal artery.

Descending branch of left colic artery.description: Lower branch of the left colic artery (from the inferior mesenteric artery). It supplies the lower descending colon and anastomoses with the uppermost sigmoid artery to continue the marginal artery.

Ileocolic artery.description:
The last branch from the right side of the superior mesenteric artery, running down and to the right to the ileocaecal junction. Its colic, anterior and posterior caecal, ileal and appendicular branches supply the terminal ileum, caecum, appendix and beginning of the ascending colon.
The appendicular artery is an end artery, which is why an obstructed, inflamed appendix readily becomes gangrenous; the ileocolic vessels are divided in a right hemicolectomy.

Marginal artery.description:
The marginal artery (of Drummond): a continuous arterial arcade along the mesenteric border of the colon, formed by anastomoses between the ileocolic, right, middle and left colic and sigmoid arteries. Vasa recta pass from it to the bowel wall.
It links the superior and inferior mesenteric territories, but is often thin near the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point), a watershed zone prone to ischaemic colitis.

Superior anorectal artery.description: The superior rectal artery: continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery after it crosses the left common iliac vessels. It descends in the root of the sigmoid mesocolon and divides into right and left branches that supply the rectum and the anal canal above the pectinate line, anastomosing with the middle and inferior rectal arteries.

Calcaneal branches of fibular artery.description: The lateral calcaneal branches of the fibular artery, which pass behind the lateral malleolus to the lateral side and back of the heel. They join the calcaneal branches of the posterior tibial artery in the calcaneal anastomosis.

Calcaneal branches of posterior tibial a.description: The medial calcaneal branches of the posterior tibial artery, which pierce the flexor retinaculum to supply the skin and fat pad of the medial and plantar heel, joining the calcaneal branches of the fibular artery.

Common interosseous artery.description: Short trunk arising from the ulnar artery just below the radial tuberosity. It passes back toward the interosseous membrane and divides into the anterior and posterior interosseous arteries, which supply the deep flexor and extensor compartments of the forearm.

Posterior interosseous artery.description: Terminal branch of the common interosseous artery that passes back above the interosseous membrane into the posterior compartment of the forearm, emerging between supinator and abductor pollicis longus. It runs down between the superficial and deep extensors with the posterior interosseous nerve, supplies them, and anastomoses with the anterior interosseous artery at the dorsal carpal network. It is the pedicle of the posterior interosseous flap.

Recurrent interosseous artery.description: Branch of the posterior interosseous artery that ascends behind the elbow between the lateral epicondyle and olecranon, deep to anconeus, to anastomose with the middle collateral branch of the profunda brachii in the elbow anastomosis.

Common palmar digital arteries.description: Three arteries that run distally from the convexity of the superficial palmar arch over the 2nd to 4th lumbricals. Each is joined by a palmar metacarpal artery from the deep arch and divides at the web space into two proper palmar digital arteries that run along adjacent sides of the fingers.

Palmar carpal branch of radial artery.description: Small branch of the radial artery given off at the lower border of pronator quadratus. It runs medially across the front of the wrist to join the palmar carpal branch of the ulnar artery, forming the palmar carpal arch that supplies the carpal bones and joints.

Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery.description: Branch of the ulnar artery arising just above the pisiform. It winds backward deep to the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris to reach the back of the wrist and joins the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery in the dorsal carpal network.

Dorsal carpal anastomosis.description: The dorsal carpal network (rete): an arterial arch on the back of the carpus formed by the dorsal carpal branches of the radial and ulnar arteries, joined by the anterior and posterior interosseous arteries. It gives off the 2nd to 4th dorsal metacarpal arteries and supplies the dorsal carpal bones, including the distal scaphoid.

Superior ulnar collateral artery.description: Branch of the brachial artery near the middle of the arm that accompanies the ulnar nerve through the medial intermuscular septum to the back of the medial epicondyle. It anastomoses with the posterior ulnar recurrent artery and helps supply the ulnar nerve at the elbow.

Ulnar recurrent artery.description: Anterior and posterior ulnar recurrent arteries arise from the ulnar artery just below the elbow. The anterior branch ascends in front of the medial epicondyle to meet the inferior ulnar collateral artery; the posterior branch runs behind the medial epicondyle with the ulnar nerve, between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, to meet the superior ulnar collateral artery.

First posterior intercostal artery.description: Posterior intercostal artery of the first intercostal space. Unlike the lower ones it does not come from the aorta but from the supreme intercostal artery (a branch of the costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery); it runs in the costal groove of the first rib with its vein and nerve.

Second posterior intercostal artery.description: Posterior intercostal artery of the second intercostal space, usually a branch of the supreme intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk. It runs in the costal groove between the posterior intercostal vein above and the intercostal nerve below and anastomoses anteriorly with the anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery.

Supreme intercostal artery.description: The superior intercostal artery: descending branch of the costocervical trunk (from the second part of the subclavian artery). It passes in front of the necks of the first two ribs, lateral to the cervicothoracic (stellate) ganglion, and gives the posterior intercostal arteries of the first and second spaces.

Frontal branch of superficial temporal a.description:
Anterior terminal branch of the superficial temporal artery that runs tortuously upward and forward over the temple and forehead. It supplies the scalp and frontalis and anastomoses with the supra-orbital and supratrochlear arteries.
Its often visibly tortuous course in the elderly makes it the usual biopsy site in suspected giant cell (temporal) arteritis.

Superior lateral genicular artery.description: Branch of the popliteal artery that curves around the femur just above the lateral condyle, deep to the tendon of biceps femoris. It supplies the vastus lateralis, the knee joint and the patella and joins the genicular anastomosis around the knee.

Inferior lateral genicular artery.description: Branch of the popliteal artery that runs laterally above the head of the fibula, deep to the lateral collateral ligament, to reach the front of the knee. It supplies the knee joint and lateral meniscus and contributes to the genicular anastomosis.

Intrarenal arteries of left kidney.description:
The branching arterial tree inside the kidney: the renal artery gives five segmental arteries (superior, anterosuperior, anteroinferior, inferior and posterior), which divide into interlobar arteries between the renal pyramids, arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary junction, and interlobular (cortical radiate) arteries that give the afferent arterioles of the glomeruli.
Segmental arteries are end arteries, so their occlusion causes a wedge-shaped infarct; the avascular plane between anterior and posterior segments (Brödel's line) guides surgical incisions.

Intrarenal arteries of right kidney.description:
The branching arterial tree inside the kidney: the renal artery gives five segmental arteries (superior, anterosuperior, anteroinferior, inferior and posterior), which divide into interlobar arteries between the renal pyramids, arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary junction, and interlobular (cortical radiate) arteries that give the afferent arterioles of the glomeruli.
Segmental arteries are end arteries, so their occlusion causes a wedge-shaped infarct; the avascular plane between anterior and posterior segments (Brödel's line) guides surgical incisions.

Intrarenal veins of left kidney.description: Veins draining the kidney: peritubular capillaries and vasa recta drain into interlobular, arcuate and interlobar veins that unite at the renal sinus to form the renal vein. Unlike the arteries, intrarenal veins are not segmental and anastomose freely, so the occlusion of one does not infarct the parenchyma.

Intrarenal veins of right kidney.description: Veins draining the kidney: peritubular capillaries and vasa recta drain into interlobular, arcuate and interlobar veins that unite at the renal sinus to form the renal vein. Unlike the arteries, intrarenal veins are not segmental and anastomose freely, so the occlusion of one does not infarct the parenchyma.

Left ascending lumbar vein.description: Longitudinal vein that runs up in front of the lumbar transverse processes, behind psoas major, linking the left common iliac, iliolumbar and lumbar veins. At the level of T12 it joins the left subcostal vein to form the hemi-azygos vein, providing a collateral route from the inferior to the superior vena cava.

Right ascending lumbar vein.description: Longitudinal vein that runs up in front of the lumbar transverse processes, behind psoas major, linking the right common iliac and lumbar veins. It joins the right subcostal vein to form the azygos vein, a collateral path between the inferior and superior venae cavae when the IVC is obstructed.

Left subcostal vein.description: Vein accompanying the subcostal artery and nerve below the twelfth rib. It unites with the left ascending lumbar vein to form the hemi-azygos vein.

Right subcostal vein.description: Vein accompanying the subcostal artery and nerve below the twelfth rib. It unites with the right ascending lumbar vein to form the azygos vein.

Left superior intercostal vein.description: Vein formed by the posterior intercostal veins of the 2nd to 3rd (or 4th) left spaces. It runs forward across the left side of the aortic arch - between the phrenic nerve in front and the vagus behind - to drain into the left brachiocephalic vein; it may communicate with the accessory hemi-azygos vein. On a chest film it can form a small nipple on the aortic knob.

Right superior intercostal vein.description: Vein formed by the posterior intercostal veins of the 2nd to 3rd (or 4th) right spaces. It descends beside the vertebral bodies and drains into the arch of the azygos vein.

Right superior phrenic vein.description: Small vein from the upper (thoracic) surface of the right half of the diaphragm that drains toward the azygos system and the pericardiacophrenic veins, accompanying the superior phrenic artery.

Left superior pulmonary vein.description:
Drains oxygenated blood from the left upper lobe including the lingula (apicoposterior, anterior and lingular veins) into the upper left part of the left atrium. It lies in front of and below the left pulmonary artery in the hilum.
The pulmonary vein ostia are the commonest origin of triggers for atrial fibrillation and are electrically isolated in catheter ablation.

Left inferior pulmonary vein.description: Drains the left lower lobe (superior vein of the lower lobe and common basal vein) into the lower left part of the left atrium. It is the lowest structure of the left hilum and lies in the pulmonary ligament, which must be divided to reach it at lobectomy.

Right superior pulmonary vein.description: Drains the right upper lobe (apical, anterior and posterior veins) and, usually, the middle lobe vein into the left atrium. It passes behind the superior vena cava; a sinus venosus atrial septal defect is often associated with its anomalous drainage into the SVC.

Right inferior pulmonary vein.description: Drains the right lower lobe - the superior vein (of segment S6) and the common basal vein - into the lower right part of the left atrium. It is the lowest element of the right hilum, lying within the pulmonary ligament.

Superior lobar artery of right lung.description: The truncus anterior: the first branch of the right pulmonary artery, arising within the pericardium or at the hilum in front of the right main bronchus. It supplies the right upper lobe through its apical, anterior and (often) posterior segmental arteries.

Middle lobar artery of right lung.description: Branch of the interlobar part of the right pulmonary artery, arising opposite the superior segmental artery of the lower lobe. It divides into lateral and medial segmental arteries that follow the bronchi of the middle lobe.

Inferior lobar artery of right lung.description: Continuation of the right interlobar pulmonary artery below the origin of the middle lobar artery. It gives the superior segmental artery (S6) and then the basal segmental arteries (medial, anterior, lateral and posterior) to the right lower lobe.

Apical segmental artery of right lung.description: Branch of the superior lobar artery (truncus anterior) supplying the apical segment (S1) of the right upper lobe. Like other segmental pulmonary arteries it runs alongside and slightly posterior to its segmental bronchus, at the centre of the bronchopulmonary segment.

Anterior segmental artery of right lung.description: Branch of the superior lobar artery (truncus anterior) that follows the anterior segmental bronchus into the anterior segment (S3) of the right upper lobe. Segmental arteries run with the bronchi in the centre of each segment, whereas the veins run between segments.

Posterior segmental artery of right lung.description: Pulmonary artery branch to the posterior segment (S2) of the right upper lobe; it arises from the truncus anterior or, as a recurrent (ascending) branch, from the interlobar artery. It accompanies the posterior segmental bronchus.

Lateral segmental artery of right lung.description: Branch of the middle lobar artery accompanying the lateral segmental bronchus into the lateral segment (S4) of the right middle lobe.

Medial segmental artery of right lung.description: Branch of the middle lobar artery accompanying the medial segmental bronchus into the medial segment (S5) of the right middle lobe, which lies against the right heart border.

Superior segmental artery of right lung.description: Branch of the right interlobar/inferior lobar artery supplying the superior segment (S6) of the right lower lobe. S6 is the most posterior and dependent segment in a supine patient, a classic site of aspiration pneumonia.

Medial basal segmental artery of right l.description: Branch of the inferior lobar artery supplying the medial basal (cardiac) segment (S7) of the right lower lobe, beside the inferior vena cava and heart.

Anterior basal segmental artery of right.description: Branch of the inferior lobar artery following the anterior basal bronchus into the anterior basal segment (S8) of the right lower lobe.

Lateral basal segmental artery of right.description: Branch of the inferior lobar artery following the lateral basal bronchus into the lateral basal segment (S9) of the right lower lobe.

Posterior basal segmental artery of righ.description: Branch of the inferior lobar artery following the posterior basal bronchus into the posterior basal segment (S10) of the right lower lobe, the most dependent segment in the upright position.

Superior lobar artery of left lung.description: The pulmonary artery branches to the left upper lobe. The left pulmonary artery arches over the left main bronchus and gives a variable number of upper-lobe branches (apicoposterior, anterior and lingular) rather than a single trunk.

Inferior lobar artery of left lung.description: The descending (interlobar) part of the left pulmonary artery, running down behind the left main and lower lobe bronchi. It gives the superior segmental artery (S6) and the basal segmental arteries of the left lower lobe.

Apical segmental artery of left lung.description: Branch of the left pulmonary artery supplying the apical part of the apicoposterior segment (S1+2) of the left upper lobe, accompanying the apicoposterior bronchus.

Posterior segmental artery of left lung.description: Branch of the left pulmonary artery supplying the posterior part of the apicoposterior segment (S1+2) of the left upper lobe. On the left the apical and posterior segments share a single segmental bronchus.

Anterior segmental artery of left lung.description: Branch of the left pulmonary artery following the anterior segmental bronchus into the anterior segment (S3) of the left upper lobe.

Superior lingular artery of left lung.description: Branch of the left pulmonary artery supplying the superior lingular segment (S4) of the left upper lobe. The lingula is the left-sided counterpart of the right middle lobe.

Inferior lingular artery of left lung.description: Branch of the left pulmonary artery supplying the inferior lingular segment (S5) of the left upper lobe, which lies against the left heart border; consolidation here effaces the left cardiac silhouette on a frontal chest film.

Superior segmental artery of left lung.description: Branch of the left inferior lobar artery supplying the superior segment (S6) of the left lower lobe, the most posterior segment in a supine patient.

Medial basal segmental artery of left lu.description: Branch of the left inferior lobar artery supplying the medial basal part of the anteromedial basal segment (S7+8) of the left lower lobe; on the left the medial and anterior basal segments usually share a bronchus.

Anterior basal segmental artery of left.description: Branch of the left inferior lobar artery following the anteromedial basal bronchus into the anterior basal segment (S8) of the left lower lobe.

Lateral basal segmental artery of left l.description: Branch of the left inferior lobar artery following the lateral basal bronchus into the lateral basal segment (S9) of the left lower lobe.

Posterior basal segmental artery of left.description: Branch of the left inferior lobar artery following the posterior basal bronchus into the posterior basal segment (S10) of the left lower lobe.

Apical vein of right lung.description: Tributary of the right superior pulmonary vein draining the apical segment (S1) of the right upper lobe. Pulmonary veins run in the intersegmental planes, between bronchopulmonary segments, and serve as surgical landmarks for segmentectomy.

Anterior vein of right lung.description: Tributary of the right superior pulmonary vein draining the anterior segment (S3) of the right upper lobe, running in the intersegmental planes.

Posterior vein of right lung.description: Tributary of the right superior pulmonary vein draining the posterior segment (S2) of the right upper lobe; it runs behind the upper lobe bronchi in the intersegmental plane.

Lateral vein of right lung.description: The lateral part of the middle lobe vein, draining the lateral segment (S4) of the right middle lobe into the right superior pulmonary vein.

Medial vein of right lung.description: The medial part of the middle lobe vein, draining the medial segment (S5) of the right middle lobe into the right superior pulmonary vein.

Superior vein of right lung.description: The superior vein of the right lower lobe, draining the superior segment (S6) into the right inferior pulmonary vein.

Superior basal vein of right lung.description: Tributary of the common basal vein draining the anterior and part of the lateral basal segments of the right lower lobe into the right inferior pulmonary vein.

Inferior basal vein of right lung.description: Tributary of the common basal vein draining the posterior and lateral basal segments of the right lower lobe into the right inferior pulmonary vein.

Anterior vein of left lung.description: Tributary of the left superior pulmonary vein draining the anterior segment (S3) of the left upper lobe, running in the intersegmental planes.

Apicoposterior vein of left lung.description: Tributary of the left superior pulmonary vein draining the apicoposterior segment (S1+2) of the left upper lobe.

Lingular vein of left lung.description: Vein formed by the superior and inferior lingular veins, draining the lingula of the left upper lobe into the left superior pulmonary vein.

Superior lingular vein of left lung.description: Tributary of the lingular vein draining the superior lingular segment (S4) of the left upper lobe.

Inferior lingular vein of left lung.description: Tributary of the lingular vein draining the inferior lingular segment (S5) of the left upper lobe.

Superior vein of left lung.description: The superior vein of the left lower lobe, draining the superior segment (S6) into the left inferior pulmonary vein.

Superior basal vein of left lung.description: Tributary of the common basal vein draining the anteromedial and lateral basal segments of the left lower lobe into the left inferior pulmonary vein.

Inferior basal vein of left lung.description: Tributary of the common basal vein draining the posterior and lateral basal segments of the left lower lobe into the left inferior pulmonary vein.

Left testicular artery.description: Long, slender branch of the abdominal aorta arising at about L2, just below the renal arteries. It runs down retroperitoneally on psoas major, crossing in front of the ureter, and passes through the deep inguinal ring to travel in the spermatic cord to the testis. Its course reflects the testis's embryonic origin in the upper posterior abdomen.

Right testicular artery.description: Long, slender branch of the abdominal aorta arising at about L2, just below the renal arteries. On the right it passes in front of the inferior vena cava, then runs down on psoas major, crossing the ureter, to enter the spermatic cord at the deep inguinal ring and supply the testis and epididymis.

Left testicular vein.description: Formed from the pampiniform plexus of the spermatic cord, it ascends on psoas major and drains at a right angle into the left renal vein. This longer course, the right-angled entry and the renal vein's passage between aorta and superior mesenteric artery are why varicoceles are far more common on the left; a new left varicocele in an adult should prompt a search for a left renal tumour.

Right testicular vein.description: Formed from the pampiniform plexus, it ascends on psoas major and enters the inferior vena cava obliquely, just below the right renal vein. An isolated right-sided varicocele is unusual and may signal IVC obstruction.

Lingual vein.description: Drains the tongue: the dorsal lingual veins, the deep lingual vein (visible through the thin mucosa under the tongue, the route of sublingual drug absorption) and the vena comitans of the hypoglossal nerve unite near the hyoid bone and drain into the internal jugular vein, directly or via the common facial vein.

Medial circumflex femoral artery.description:
Usually a branch of the profunda femoris artery. It passes backward between pectineus and iliopsoas, then between obturator externus and adductor brevis, to reach the back of the femoral neck.
Its deep branch gives the retinacular arteries that run up the neck under the synovium and are the main blood supply to the femoral head; they are torn in displaced intracapsular femoral neck fractures, causing avascular necrosis. It also joins the cruciate anastomosis.

Perforating femoral arteries.description: Usually three perforating arteries from the profunda femoris (the fourth is its terminal part). They pierce adductor brevis and adductor magnus close to the linea aspera to reach the posterior compartment, supplying the hamstrings and vastus lateralis and forming a longitudinal chain of anastomoses; the first joins the cruciate anastomosis.

Mental branch of inferior alveolar arter.description: Terminal branch of the inferior alveolar artery that leaves the mandible through the mental foramen with the mental nerve, supplying the chin and lower lip and anastomosing with the inferior labial and submental arteries.

Mylohyoid branch of inferior alveolar ar.description: Small branch given off by the inferior alveolar artery just before it enters the mandibular foramen. It runs in the mylohyoid groove with the nerve to mylohyoid and supplies the mylohyoid muscle.

Occipital sinus.description: The smallest dural venous sinus, lying in the attached margin of the falx cerebelli. It begins near the foramen magnum, where it communicates with the marginal sinuses and vertebral venous plexuses, and ascends to the confluence of sinuses. It can be large in children and must be considered in posterior fossa surgery.

Pectoral branches of thoraco-acromial ar.description: Branches of the thoraco-acromial trunk (from the second part of the axillary artery) that run between pectoralis major and minor, supplying both muscles and the breast, and anastomosing with the lateral thoracic and intercostal arteries. They form the vascular pedicle of the pectoralis major flap used in head and neck reconstruction.

Perforating branches of plantar metatars.description: Communicating vessels between the plantar and dorsal arterial systems of the foot. Posterior perforating branches pass through the proximal intermetatarsal spaces from the deep plantar arch to the dorsal metatarsal arteries; anterior perforating branches join the plantar and dorsal metatarsal arteries near the web spaces.

Short posterior ciliary arteries.description:
About 10-20 small branches of the ophthalmic artery (via the posterior ciliary arteries) that pierce the sclera in a ring around the optic nerve. They supply the choroid, the outer retina and, through the circle of Zinn-Haller, the optic nerve head.
Their occlusion, classically in giant cell arteritis, causes anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy and sudden painless visual loss.

Spinal branch of iliolumbar artery.description: Small branch of the lumbar part of the iliolumbar artery that enters the intervertebral foramen between L5 and the sacrum, supplying the cauda equina, spinal meninges and vertebral body.

Superficial branch of medial plantar art.description: Small branch of the medial plantar artery that runs forward along the medial side of the sole to supply the medial side of the great toe, often joining the first plantar or dorsal metatarsal artery.

Deep branch of transverse cervical arter.description: Descending branch of the transverse cervical artery that runs down along the medial border of the scapula with the dorsal scapular nerve, deep to levator scapulae and the rhomboids. When it arises directly from the subclavian artery it is called the dorsal scapular artery. It contributes to the scapular anastomosis.

Superficial branch of transverse cervica.description: The superficial cervical artery: ascending branch of the transverse cervical artery that runs under trapezius with the accessory nerve, supplying trapezius and the surrounding muscles and lymph nodes.

Superior mesenteric vein.description:
Drains the small intestine, caecum, appendix, ascending and transverse colon, and the head of the pancreas. It runs in the root of the mesentery to the right of the superior mesenteric artery, crosses the third part of the duodenum and the uncinate process, and joins the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein.
Its relation to the artery is checked on imaging for malrotation; mesenteric venous thrombosis causes venous bowel ischaemia.

Superior thyroid vein.description: Drains the upper pole of the thyroid gland, running with the superior thyroid artery, and empties into the internal jugular vein (or common facial vein). It is ligated with the superior pole vessels at thyroidectomy.

Supra-orbital artery.description: Branch of the ophthalmic artery that runs forward above levator palpebrae superioris and leaves the orbit through the supra-orbital notch or foramen with the supra-orbital nerve. It supplies the forehead and scalp and anastomoses with the supratrochlear and superficial temporal arteries, a link between the internal and external carotid systems.
